doc.title: Greg Caputo interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 14, 1998

chapter: Views on drummers and the state of jazz
title: Favorite drummers, learning from students and Tony Williams
summary: He has no favorites, learns from students and even a broken washing machine, and learned hi-hat use from Tony Williams.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Now let’s see you’ve mentioned Buddy Rich and Gene Krupa and Joe Morello. Who is the player that you like to listen to who you would consider, oh let’s say the most modern?

I’ve heard maybe Gene Krupa in his recordings come up with something what I would consider modern. My next door neighbor plays drums, and he’s played some things that I will borrow shall we say. Everybody has something to offer. I really don’t have any favorites. I listen to everybody and help everybody I can. It’s just ongoing, that’s the way I think it should be, everybody helping and I have no favorites. One of my students, who might take his third lesson, “Well I’ve been practicing this, what do you think?” And it will just astound me, what a great lick. I can use this. So my students are my favorite drummers. My washing machine last week broke, the bearings went and it had this great sound with this blanket in it. And I wrote it down before I unplugged it because it turned out something, I said I can apply that. So I listen to everything, not only drummers but sounds.
Wow. Was the washing machine in four?
No actually I think it was nine-eight but you know, it’s something that I can use, and I got it down and I’ll work on it, and I’ll throw it into a four bar lick somewhere along the line.
That’s great. It’s neat to hear. People like Tony Williams, those kind of drummers, do you enjoy them also?

Yes, a master, definitely. Taught me how to use the hi-hat listening to him, and he played the hi-hat on all four, and I do that sometimes — sometimes too, I’ll wake up the bass player, or to calm them down, because that’ll draw, it draws attention without slamming down a bass drum, so I would use that technique sometimes with a piano player. So I use a jazz technique in a big band, so I pull from him, definitely a master, a powerful, powerful drummer. So sad that he left us so early.
